articles.title: Roger Goodell Says NFL Is Looking into Whether to Punish 49ers Owner Jed York Following His Arrest
articles.summary: SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — Commissioner Roger Goodell said the NFL is looking into whether San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York will be punished for violating the league's personal conduct policy after he was caught in a prostitution sting in Ohio.
articles.body:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — Commissioner Roger Goodell said the NFL is looking into whether San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York will be punished for violating the league's personal conduct policy after he was caught in a prostitution sting in Ohio.

"It's being reviewed under the personal conduct policy," Goodell said Wednesday at the owners' meetings in Atlanta. "We'll do that and when there's something to be reported we'll talk."

York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute.

Predicting When Injured Stars Will Debut

York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to the an undercover online prostitution advertisement.

He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He also was fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York and that was later given to the human trafficking task force as part of the plea. York also completed an online course.

York has spent most of the summer in Ohio, where he grew up near Youngstown. He had filed for divorce from his wife, Danielle, in May, according to court records.

Owners have been previously punished for violating the personal conduct policy. The late Indianapolis Colts owner Jim Irsay was suspended for six games and fined $500,000 following a guilty plea to driving while impaired in 2014.

New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was investigated but not punished by the league after he was arrested in Florida in 2019 for allegedly paying for sex with a woman at a massage parlor. The charge was later dropped after a court ruled that police violated the rights of Kraft and the other customers when they secretly installed video cameras inside massage rooms at the spa.

York was arrested on Sunday in East Palestine, Ohio, and pleaded guilty on Monday to two misdemeanors.

articles.title: Any player who returns to college football can't sign with NFL team for remainder of that year, league says
articles.summary: With players who've spent time on league rosters returning to the collegiate ranks, the NFL is attempting to clear up some confusion.
articles.body:
The adoption of a new college eligibility system — an age-based, five-year model designed to eliminate waivers, redshirts and roster logjams created by a surge of athletes in their mid-20s sticking in school — has been furiously challenged in the courts by members of the 2022 high school class who want a fifth year of eligibility.

The new eligibility system, which is replacing one that allowed four seasons of competition over five years with no age restrictions, excludes student-athletes who exhausted their eligibility during the 2025-26 academic year.

That bucket is filled with athletes who first enrolled in 2022, following high school graduation. As of an Aug. 21 report from Yahoo Sports' Ross Dellenger , more than 150 athletes had filed a total of 18 lawsuits across 15 states. Wins against the NCAA in state courts have allowed athletes to return to college, including football players who were in NFL training camps this offseason.

The phenomenon has bewildered NFL coaches , and, as reported by ESPN's Adam Schefter , the league clarified its eligibility rules on Wednesday.

Here's the memo the NFL sent, via Schefter:

If a player signed to an NFL contract is cut, he may return to college football, "subject to applicable NCAA eligibility rules," the memo reads.

Notably, any player who returns to college football can't join an NFL team for the remainder of that year.

"An NFL Club that signs such a player is subject to discipline by the Commissioner, including the loss of draft selections and negotiating rights to the player involved," the memo reads.

The memo also states: "… Club personnel are prohibited from entering into any undisclosed agreement or understanding with any player or player affiliate (including player agents) involving consideration to a player. This prohibition includes any agreement or understanding regarding the player's future status or opportunity to return to the Club after playing elsewhere during the 2026 season. Violations may subject Clubs to the loss of draft choices and/or fines, and Club personnel may also be subject to fines and/or suspension."

Even though a path has opened momentarily for high school class of 2022 athletes to make their way back to college for a final season of eligibility, conferences are enacting policy to prevent member institutions from rostering at least some of those athletes.

The Big Ten and SEC are chief among them .

The SEC, for instance, announced Tuesday that its institutions are not permitted to have an athlete on its roster who has previously declared for the NFL, NBA or WNBA Draft and didn't appropriately withdraw. The conference is also banning athletes who signed a contract with a team in a pro football league, including the NFL, or a team in the NBA/G League or WNBA. Those who have been listed on a pro football league roster, or that of an NBA/G League team or a WNBA team are prohibited as well.

The SEC noted that penalties will be enforced against member institutions that don't comply. As for the Big Ten, per On3's Pete Nakos , member institutions who violate its policy will face a coach suspension of 50% of contests and an institutional fine.

The Big Ten's policy applies only to football players who have signed a pro contract, were on a pro roster or declared for the NFL Draft as an underclassman without withdrawing. But the conference is considering rules restricting pro athletes in other sports from conference competition.

articles.title: Mike Evans Injury Update, Latest on 49ers WR's Status Ahead of NFL Season, Fantasy Football Drafts
articles.summary: The San Francisco 49ers and fantasy football managers alike received some positive news regarding wide receiver Mike Evans on Wednesday.
articles.body:
The San Francisco 49ers and fantasy football managers alike received some positive news regarding wide receiver Mike Evans on Wednesday.

ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Evans plans on playing San Francisco's Week 1 game against the Los Angeles Rams even though he has dealt with injuries during training camp.

"His latest, a groin issue, is considered minor barring a change," Fowler added.

Evans' health has been a major storyline leading into the 2026 campaign, especially since injuries limited him to just eight games last season.

It was the first time in his career he failed to appear in at least 13 games in a season.

That durability is a major reason he has been so consistent since he entered the league as the No. 7 overall pick of the 2014 NFL draft. He surpassed 1,000 receiving yards in each of his first 11 years and tallied double-digit touchdown catches in six of them.

Evans will forever be a Tampa Bay Buccaneers legend because of that production, but the 2026 season is his first with a different team. And while it is unrealistic to expect him to post career-best numbers in what will be his age-33 season, he is quite important to San Francisco's aerial attack.

After all, Ricky Pearsall is out for the season with injury, and Brandon Aiyuk is not someone who is going to play for the team. That leaves Evans and Deebo Samuel, who joined the team this offseason, as the top options in the wide receiver room along with rookie De'Zhaun Stribling.

Tight end George Kittle also figures to be a major part of the passing game, but he is coming off a torn Achilles and is still something of a question mark.

Evans will need to provide some answers for the 49ers if they are going to live up to their potential and challenge the Rams and the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC West. That makes it all the more important to have him on the field, and it seems like San Francisco will have him available at the start of the season.

articles.title: Roger Goodell Explains Why Pro Bowl Will Be Eliminated, Game is Not 'Up to NFL standards'
articles.summary: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell explained why the Pro Bowl will no longer be played moving forward.
articles.body:
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell explained why the Pro Bowl will no longer be played moving forward.

"I think we've been focused on the game," Goodell said Wednesday, per Mark Maske of Front Office Sports. "You've heard me say it for many years about the quality of the game in the Pro Bowl. I don't think it's up to NFL standards. And that's why we changed to the flag game several years ago. So I'm not sure the last time you want to say we played a game in a football sense. So I think this is something that we talked to our players about, the Pro Bowl players in particular. We had conference calls the last couple years: What's working? What's not? What would you like to see? And the number one thing that came out—and there were a lot of wonderful comments by the players—one is: 'We want to be honored and celebrated as a Pro Bowl player.'… It just opened my eyes. I never really thought about it in the context of that."

"It's not honoring the replacement players," he added. "It's honoring the guys who are selected by the fans, by the players, by the coaches. And so that was really the core of it, is: How do we do this in the right way? And our players, you know, they did what they normally do. They had great recommendations on how to do that. And second, a willingness to lead that the all-star format doesn't really work for our game…. It's something that we felt strongly about. And I think our players, they deserve to be celebrated when they get the Pro Bowl honor."

On Wednesday, NFL executives presented team owners with the future of the Pro Bowl that doesn't include any game or competition.

According to Jonathan Jones of The Athletic, 88 players will be selected for the Pro Bowl with no alternates following the update. Pro Bowlers will now receive an invitation to Los Angeles for an in-person celebration in February rather than participating in a game.

The Pro Bowl format was changed multiple times prior to its elimination, switching from a traditional game to days of skills challenges that culminated in a flag football contest in 2023.

Now, the Pro Bowl will only exist as an individual performance honor that players can earn.

articles.title: After 75 years the Pro Bowl is dead: Here's what replaces the game nobody wanted to watch
articles.summary: NFL News: The NFL officially ended the Pro Bowl game on Wednesday, closing out a 75-year tradition that had slowly lost the plot. The league announced at its ow.
articles.body: The NFL officially ended the Pro Bowl game on Wednesday, closing out a 75-year tradition that had slowly lost the plot. The league announced at its owners meeting in Atlanta that no game will be played after this season. Players selected as Pro Bowlers will still receive the honor and gather in Los Angeles for a celebration, but the actual football game is gone. This is not a pause. The NFL is not regrouping. It is a full stop on what had become the most skippable event on the sports calendar.Why did the NFL cancel the Pro Bowl game?The honest answer is that the players stopped caring, and the league finally admitted it out loud. NFL executive vice president of football operations Troy Vincent spoke directly with more than a dozen star players this summer, and what he heard was consistent. They did not want competitive football after the playoffs ended. Vincent put it plainly at the owners meeting: "You come off the championship games and the viewers see the physicality of the game and you try to replicate that. Frankly, it just doesn't sit well. This isn't a good representation."That admission matters more than it might seem. For years the NFL kept pushing the format, hoping a tweak would fix the problem. The game moved out of Honolulu, the home it had for decades. In 2023 the league switched entirely to flag football, hoping the casual format would generate energy. It did not. Ratings stayed soft. Players showed up out of obligation, not excitement. Nobody was fooled.Peter O'Reilly, the NFL's executive vice president overseeing events, framed the decision with uncommon directness. "It's OK to be the first league to walk away from a competitive all-star game," he said in Atlanta. That line will not make headlines for its poetry, but it signals something real: the NFL is no longer interested in defending a product it cannot fix.What happens to the Pro Bowl now that the game is gone?The title survives. The game does not. The NFL confirmed that 88 players will still earn Pro Bowl recognition after this season and be honored at an event in Los Angeles. Several flag football exhibitions will take place around that time, though they will serve as entertainment rather than competition. The core distinction, being named one of the best at your position in the NFL, stays intact.The league also eliminated replacement selections going forward. In the past, injured players or Super Bowl participants were swapped out for alternates, which diluted the honor. Cleveland Browns rookie quarterback Shedeur Sanders made the Pro Bowl this year as a replacement. Under the new structure, that category is gone. If a player earns it, they earn it outright.O'Reilly explained the thinking behind the restructured honor: "The Pro Bowl has always been about recognizing the players who distinguish themselves as the very best in the NFL. A Pro Bowl selection will return to its original purpose, honoring the best of the best. We want that distinction to carry even greater meaning for the players, their families, their clubs and our fans."The voting process stays the same: an equal split between players, coaches, and fans. What changes is the weight behind it. Without a game to water things down, a Pro Bowl selection becomes a cleaner acknowledgment of a great season rather than a footnote to an event most people forgot was happening.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: As Eagles adopt more aggressive offense, Jalen Hurts 'not afraid of making mistakes'
articles.summary: The Eagles have lost several offensive coordinators over the first five years of Hurts' starting career. This year, Sean Mannion brings in a system that's to...
articles.body:
PHILADELPHIA — Two weeks later, the tweet had surpassed 17 million views. And that's just how far it traveled on one of the Philadelphia Eagles ' social media platforms.

The Eagles had posted to X a video trumpeting a practice interception by 2024 first-round draft pick Quinyon Mitchell . A vigorous debate broke out.

Was the video — which spotlighted quarterback Jalen Hurts ' throwing mechanics in its narrow, vertical framing — yet another reason to wonder whether Hurts is headed the way of his predecessor Carson Wentz , whom the Eagles moved on from more suddenly than most NFL teams would have?

Or was the video a totally reasonable chance to spotlight a sharp defensive highlight in a world that is increasingly trending toward offense? Its "Right on Q" caption directed fans to Mitchell, who picked off the pass that appeared to be intended for Hollywood Brown . But corners of the internet can turn just about anything into a slight.

Fast forward to Wednesday, 14 days after the tweet but less than 24 hours removed from the Eagle's lone public practice at their stadium. This time, offseason acquisition Riq Woolen intercepted two of Hurts' passes, including one he returned for a touchdown.

And left tackle Jordan Mailata had thoughts.

"Everyone's talking about all the picks and stuff, but it's not about that," Mailata told Yahoo Sports, when asked not about the interception but Hurts' training camp plan more generally. "It's: Is he executing what coach is trying to get him to do? And he is. And I think before, he would be a little hesitant to be like that, but now there's no fear. … This year, he's not afraid of making mistakes.

"When you're learning something new, that's how you have to be. You got to have thick skin."

Hurts is also adjusting to his sixth play-caller entering his seventh NFL season — a wild rate of turnover even in an impatient league. ( Go back to high school and college, and Hurts is on his 11th play caller in 12 years .)

The Eagles have lost some coordinators to head coaching jobs (Shane Steichen, Kellen Moore) and others after recent struggles (Kevin Patullo, Brian Johnson). But across the first five years of Hurts' starting career, Philadelphia cycled through coordinators bringing similar schemes.

This year, Mannion's introduction of Shanahan-McVay system principles are totally different.

The Eagles know they're taking a risk, both on a first-time coordinator and on their players adapting to different techniques and formations quickly enough to compete come their regular-season opener against the Washington Commanders . But the risk is part of the point, head coach Nick Sirianni said. And the club is eager to see whether it pays off.

"I wouldn't trade our last five years with any other coach or any other team in the entire NFL," Sirianni told Yahoo Sports on Wednesday. "It was just time to switch. … There was enough junk being thrown around on defense to stop the things that we were doing where we needed a little bit of a change that handles a little bit more junk.

"We need things that are better suited to handle junk."

In Eagles' new offense, 'everything's aggressive'

Mailata long thought the Eagles' offensive line he's helped anchor the last six years was aggressive. Since Mannion's arrival, he's changed his mind.

"I've never really thought about and never knew that life could be like this as an O-lineman," Mailata said. "Just being more into the line, more aggressive and getting your hands, shooting your hands. We've always been [about] pretty patient punches in the pass game.

"Now it's like everything from the run game to the pass game to the play-action game, everything's aggressive."

Veteran offensive linemen are being asked to shift the techniques that led to success, including two Super Bowl appearances and one championship. So are their counterparts across the offense, from Hurts to running back Saquon Barkley to a revamped receiver cast.

Change for the Eagles' offense is a feature rather than a bug. Sirianni's belief that their offense no longer best positioned players for success against modern defensive trends showed in last year's statistics.

After three straight years ranking top 10 in points scored and yards, the Eagles fell last year to 19th and 24th, respectively. Hurts threw for 8 more yards per game last year (201.5) in 16 starts than the year before (193.5) in 15 games.

The Eagles' run game, meanwhile, fell off a cliff to the tune of 62.4 yards fewer per game (from 179.3 in 2024 to 116.9 in 2025). The Eagles' offensive line success dropped from sixth in pass-block win rate and ninth in run-block win rate, per ESPN's advanced metrics , to 17th and 16th, respectively.

Enter their new system, which Philadelphia believes will allow Barkley to discern more information on reads that dictate his cuts. This offense is heavily predicated on timing, from quarterback footwork to receiver route depth to blocks that could make or break anticipatory throws and more regimented system choices.

The Eagles believe their wide receiver room features versatility in the wake of trading A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots on June 1 for a 2028 first-round draft pick and 2027 fifth. Former Green Bay Packers receiver Dontayvion Wicks , 2026 first-round selection Makai Lemon and journeyman 2019 first-rounder Hollywood Brown join a room led by DeVonta Smith , who's coming off his third 1,000-yard season in the last four years.

"You have a No. 1 receiver in DeVonta Smith, who, we've always believed has been a No. 1 receiver," Sirianni said. "You have a 'Tay Wicks who I think has great qualities of a wide receiver: I always think that my ideal receiver in the NFL, before I look at speed and before I look at anything else, [has] play strength and body quickness [to get] in and out of the breaks. And this guy has elite of both."

Brown and Elijah Moore will be tabbed to add further speed while Darius Cooper will step up for "dirty work," Sirianni said.

Separation at the top of routes will be imperative amid the strict timing of the system, while formations will more often feature bunch or tighter splits to disguise from defenses whether a run or pass awaits. Expect more pre-snap motion, a trend in vogue across the NFL.

Mailata endearingly called Mannion "crazy" for the level of detail he's installing.

"He's awesome," Mailata said. "It's like, 'It doesn't matter what they bring, this is what we're going to do. And I have answers.' He has answers built in for everything."

Jalen Hurts has won through his career. With new offense, will that continue?

During Tuesday's night practice, Hurts faced a quick game, or gap and path switch, from Eagles defensive linemen on his left, backup quarterback Tanner McKee said. Hurts reset and targeted an intermediate dig route to his right to save the play.

"We always talk about rhythm and tempo and getting through a progression," McKee told Yahoo Sports. "In this offense, we're not counting on one guy to be a winner. If the route's not there and the defense took it away, well then we have a good backside concept that's going to complement. So just being able to get through a progression. That he was able to do last night actually at the stadium practice, that I thought was great."

With yet another play-caller, Hurts will look to be great for another season.

In six years in Philadelphia, including five atop the depth chart, Hurt has completed 64.4% of his pass attempts for 17,891 yards, 110 touchdowns and 45 interceptions. Arguably his best stat line: He's won 56 of 78 starts in the last five seasons. Only the Buffalo Bills ' Josh Allen (60) and Kansas City Chiefs ' Patrick Mahomes (57), each regular-season MVP winners, have won more games during that time.

Wins don't arrive via quarterback alone, even if most quarterbacks and head coaches receive a disproportionate amount of credit for wins and criticism for losses. Hurts has received far more criticism through his winning seasons than he has credit. Sirianni reminds his quarterback: That does not matter.

"Outside noise doesn't really matter," Sirianni said. "How many games you've won in a row doesn't really matter. How many games you've lost in a row doesn't really matter. It's all about the work and it's always, regardless of the circumstances or regardless of the situation, is the same person every day with his work and the way he attacks a day.

"He leads so much through just the way he goes about his business."

Eagles offensive players will look to Hurts to continue leading on the field as they sort through a new and demanding offensive system not yet totally natural or familiar to most of them. Some of that leading will come through play adjustments that often fly under the radar, like the play reset Hurts made Tuesday night. Others will come through mistakes like camp interceptions — a reminder to acclimating teammates that the goal is to learn and grow more than it is to appear put-together in training camp.

Responses to mistakes often send the loudest messages. Hurts' response to his Tuesday night interceptions were an example.

"He's always been cool, calm, collected, but I like when he has that fire, when he knows he made a mistake and then he's the first one to correct it and then make a big play," Mailata said. "If you make mistakes, that's how you learn. And he's taking it with grace and he's led by example doing that and overcoming those picks because right after that was touchdowns."

articles.title: NFL champions Seattle Seahawks sold to Khosla Group for record $9.6 billion
articles.summary: The price tag is an NFL record for a franchise sale and the second-highest valuation in North American sports history.
articles.body:
The owners of the National Football League (NFL) in the United States have unanimously approved the sale of the Seattle Seahawks for a league-record price of $9.6bn to a group led by the Khosla family.

The sales agreement was announced on July 11 and awaited approval at a special meeting of the owners in Atlanta on Wednesday to become official. The sale was in accordance with the wishes of the late team owner, Paul Allen.

At least 24 of 32 owners were required to approve the sale, which was expected after the NFL’s finance and ownership policy committees voted unanimously last week to recommend ratification.

“How often do you get to buy a franchise that just won the Super Bowl? ” said the multi-billionaire businessman Vinod Khosla, standing with his coowners, wife Neeru and son Neal. “We are incredibly lucky and humbled by this gift, I would say, from the Allen trust.”

“The task ahead is actually pretty simple,” Vinod Khosla said after the vote. “Keep the winning streak alive. Get another Super Bowl. That’s simple. In general, our approach is generally going to be long-term focused. That’s our inclination always. So keep winning, take a long-term approach, and learn a lot.”

The estate of Paul G. Allen, which inherited the NFL team after his death in 2018, agreed to terms with the Khosla family after a search for a new owner. Allen’s will stipulated that the team be sold and assets be distributed to various charities.

The price tag is an NFL record for a franchise sale. It is the second-highest valuation in North American sports history; the Los Angeles Lakers sold for $10 billion last year and were more recently valued at $12.5 billion, as Bob Iger and Josh Kushner plan to purchase a majority stake in the NBA team from Mark Walter.

The Washington Commanders were sold for approximately $6 billion in 2023 to a group headed by Josh Harris.

Paul Allen bought the Seahawks for $194 million from Ken Behring in 1997 and helped keep the team in Seattle. Allen, cofounder of Microsoft, also owned the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers, with his sister Jody Allen assuming duties as owner for the estate.

Vinod Khosla thanked Jody Allen and the Allen Trust “for trusting us with this franchise”.

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said the family’s experience with the 49ers was attractive to other NFL owners.

“They know our league well,” Goodell said. “As you know, they have been in ownership in the NFC West with the San Francisco 49ers. They understand the passion of the NFL, they understand the 12s, they understand this Seattle community and the NFL. And so that makes this transaction particularly attractive to all of us.”

The 71-year-old is a venture capitalist and a limited partner of the San Francisco 49ers — buying 3.1 percent of the franchise last year at a more than $8.5 billion valuation, according to the ESPN network.

He will have to relinquish his stake in that team as part of the agreement to buy the Seahawks, as the transaction could close before the defending Super Bowl champions open the season on September 9 against the New England Patriots, the team they defeated 29-13 in February for the title.

Khosla, born in Pune, India, is the cofounder of Sun Microsystems and founder of the venture capital firm, Khosla Ventures. Neeru Khosla, who also was born in India and met Vinod when they were children, will be the controlling owner, according to The Athletic. It says their son, Neal, is expected to have a major role in the organisation.

Vinod Khosla said he was first a fan of the Pittsburgh Steelers when he moved to the United States in 1976.

“We’ve been very passionate about football for a long time,” he said. “I would say we’ve been going to home games at the 49ers since [Neal] was five, maybe half of all home games since he was five. And so football is definitely a passion. … I was originally and still am a big Steelers fan. … Little known fact, but I still watch all the Steelers games, too.”

articles.title: Lane Kiffin's NFL transfer portal brings spineless leaders to life | Opinion
articles.summary: It took ethical bankruptcy at LSU to spur action, but SEC school officials who spent years wasting clout got off their soapbox and joined fight.
articles.body:
In the joke, a disaster strikes, or a major news event happens, and a reporter hollers, Alert the media!

Buddy, you are the media, so stop hollering and start doing your job.

For the past several years, university chancellors and presidents have been like that reporter, watching college sports burn around them and hollering they need someone to save College Sports Inc. from eating itself whole.

Nobody inside the college sports enterprise persistently does less with more power than chancellors and presidents.

While university muckety-mucks begged someone, anyone — but, especially, Congress — to save them from burning themselves at the stake, they ignored the truth that they're the ones with the most authority to address college sports' issues.

Finally, it reached a boiling point. Texas Tech and LSU flouted norms so egregiously this year that presidents and chancellors across the land woke up and realized nobody is coming to save them from abdicating their responsibilities.

Mercifully, something good could come of Texas Tech's embrace of a gambling addict and Lane Kiffin's NFL dumpster diving : A "Fix It Yourself" era of college sports is showing signs of life.

Lane Kiffin's plan to embrace NFL transfer portal spurs SEC to action

You can't totally fault Kiffin (well, you can, but save your energy) for being exactly who he's repeatedly proven to be .

That's someone with a loose grip on ethics, someone who repeatedly plants his flag at the vanguard of unsavoriness, someone who'll take a mile if you give him an inch.

If another coach might think about bending or breaking a rule or ignoring conventional ethics, Kiffin will race to beat them to the starting line.

Kiffin used that rationale to justify opening LSU's door to players who'd been cut from NFL rosters. If Kiffin gets his way, Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris will join his roster as NFL castoffs turned fifth-year seniors.

Leave it to Kiffin to embrace the NFL transfer portal.

(Will Wade could make Kiffin look like a novice, but that's another kettle of fish .)

Truth is, Kiffin doesn't give a hoot about norms or rules, and he's also not the only coach looking to add pros to the roster. Never mind raiding the NFL's waiver wire is a slap in the face of college players who've been in the program practicing all offseason.

Kiffin figured these NFL retreads would spruce up his depth chart, and a state judge gave the OK for their return to college ball. That's the only green light Lane needed to see, and who was going to stop him? Certainly not the puppets in LSU's C-suites.

Left to their own devices, university presidents and chancellors are spineless, but when an issue such as this unites them across the conference, an opportunity for self-governance emerges.

NFL players returning to college? Not so fast

Following the Big Ten's lead, the SEC's membership voted in a penalty structure that would include coaching suspensions and significant institutional fines if an institution plays ex-pros from leagues like the NFL or NBA.

A lawyer will see this penalty structure cascading down from Power Four conferences as lawsuit fodder, but I see an attempt, at least, at a solution. A fix-it-ourselves mentality beats begging big government for a bailout that hasn't materialized after several years of lobbying.

Will this self-governance maneuver succeed? Don't know. Stay tuned to CourtTV.

Already, a conference's presidents and chancellors showed some teeth once before this year.

The Big 12 presidents and chancellors muscled up and brought Cody Campbell University (the institution formerly known as Texas Tech) to heel, sinking the Red Raiders ' plans to play Sorsby. After Sorsby's gambling activity got exposed, he admitted to being a sports gambling addict who trampled NCAA's black-and-white wagering rules for years. He bet on college football, including bets involving his own team.

A Texas judge nonetheless ruled Sorsby could play, despite the NCAA saying otherwise. Texas Tech President Lawrence Schovanec joined a pitiful PR campaign to try to grease the wheels for Sorsby's return. Remember, at the individual level, presidents and chancellors tend to be feckless, and too meek to apply checks on their coaches and booster class.

Banded together, though, they've got more courage, and the Big 12 united to deploy a series of governance and legal moves to scupper the Sorsby comeback.

Now, throughout Power Four conferences, presidents and chancellors are coming together to erect hurdles in the way of coaches adding NFL castoffs to NCAA rosters.

It took ethical bankruptcy at Texas Tech and LSU to spur action, but school officials who spent years wasting their clout finally decided to get off their soapbox and join the fight.

Blake Toppmeyer is the USA TODAY Network's senior national college football columnist. Email him at BToppmeyer@gannett.com and follow him on X @btoppmeyer .

articles.summary: The 49ers and Raiders are ready to wrap up their part of the NFL preseason and get going on the real thing. Here's how to watch the finale.
articles.body:
The preseason finale for the Las Vegas Raiders and San Francisco 49ers is here, and both teams have made headlines for drastically different things.

The Raiders secured the No. 1 overall pick and drafted quarterback Fernando Mendoza . In limited action, the rookie has at times looked the part, and also has shown there's still a ways to go. That much is evident and has led the Raiders to decide they'll give the QB1 job to Kirk Cousins until Mendoza is ready to go.

When Mendoza is ready to go, however, is anyone's guess. The Raiders are determined to slow-play it with their passer of the future, leading to questions of when the passer will make his Sunday debut this season.

The 49ers have eyes on a Lombardi Trophy once again, but they've had to navigate some off-the-field distractions throughout training camp, an inauspicious start to their season. First, it was Kyle Shanahan's car accident and the questions that persisted. In the month that followed, principal owner Jed York was arrested.

In between, the 49ers lost wide receiver Ricky Pearsall to a knee injury, Mike Evans dealt with bumps and bruises and substation conspiracy theories resurfaced.
